member.name: T:GameLauncher.Relay.Data.RelayDatabaseInitializer
member.summary: Creates and migrates the relay schema.

remarks.para: Every statement here is valid on both SQLite and PostgreSQL. Three rules make that possible, and breaking any of them is what would tie the relay to one engine:

item.description: No auto-increment identity columns. This is where the dialects genuinely diverge. Every key is a value the application generates — a friend code, a catalog id, a device id, or a composite of natural keys.

No defaults on boolean or timestamp columns. PostgreSQL rejects DEFAULT 0 on a boolean, and the two engines spell "now" differently. Values are always supplied by the application, which is also easier to test.
Only shared column types — TEXT, INTEGER, BOOLEAN, DOUBLE PRECISION. Timestamps are UTC ISO-8601 text, which orders lexicographically exactly as it does chronologically.

member.summary: Default .

remarks.para: Tokens are 32 cryptographically random bytes, base64url-encoded, prefixed glr_. The prefix makes a leaked token recognisable in a log or a paste.

They are stored as an unsalted SHA-256 hash. Salting plus a slow key derivation exists to make guessing expensive, and guessing is only a threat against low-entropy secrets such as human-chosen passwords. A 256-bit random token cannot be brute-forced however fast the hash is, so a slow KDF would cost a CPU-bound operation on every single request and buy nothing.

Omitting the salt is also what makes the hash a usable lookup key: the relay hashes the presented token and finds the device in one indexed read. With a per-row salt it would have to hash against every device row in turn.
